articles.summary: Moviegoers in Taiwan will be able to steer the outcome of three feature films with their phones, as interactive cinema outfit Next Interactive Studio and exhibitor Showtime Cinemas roll out a run of titles opening one after another, starting Nov. 27 with English-language survival thriller "The Run." articles.content:
Moviegoers in Taiwan will be able to steer the outcome of three feature films with their phones, as interactive cinema outfit Next Interactive Studio and exhibitor Showtime Cinemas roll out a run of titles opening one after another, starting Nov. 27 with English-language survival thriller "The Run."

Audiences scan a QR code on the screen to link their phones to a voting server in the auditorium. The majority pick at each decision point sets where the story goes next, including which characters survive and how the film ends. "The Run" is set on a remote trail in the mountains of northern Italy, where a fitness influencer with a worldwide following is pursued by masked killers. Audiences make snap decisions that decide whether she lives, and along the way bring a buried trauma to the surface. The film was cut down from 3.5 hours of footage into a theatrical version running 90 to 100 minutes, with five possible endings and 20 ways for her to die. It opens at Showtime's flagship sites in Taipei, Taichung and Kaohsiung.

Japanese live-action comedy "Back From the Other World" follows on Dec. 4. Adapted from a hit interactive game and produced with Fourth Wall, a creative team spanning Japan and Taiwan, the film is shot in the first person and casts the viewer as a hero who has slain demons in a fantasy realm, only to return to office life with his magic still working. Back at work, he discovers the goddesses he knew in that other world are now his bosses and co-workers. The cast includes Kawakita Saika and Uehara Ai. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Kaiju Princess," set for the first quarter of 2027, is a first-person romance-adventure based on a popular Taiwanese game series and made in the style of tokusatsu, the Japanese special-effects genre. Starring Momonogi Kana and Unpai, the film – subtitled "Secret Pulse" – drops audiences into a world battered by giant-monster disasters. Group votes decide how humanity fights back against alien invaders and which romantic storylines play out. Its producers are again drawn from both Japan and Taiwan.

Next Interactive is headed by founder Ronan Wong, who the company says has advised on, produced or distributed every interactive film to receive a commercial theatrical release, across both Western and Eastern markets. Wong served as interactive adviser on Japanese animated feature "Hypnosis Mic – Division Rap Battle," which grossed JPY2.7 billion ($17 million) from fewer than 100 screens.

"Interactive cinema transforms passive auditoriums into legendary, shared social arenas that simply cannot be replicated at home," Wong said.

He described the Taiwan launch as a major milestone for the company's network. "As we prepare to bring these titles and our platform to global territories in 2027, we are proving that when audiences co-create the story together, cinema becomes an unmissable collective event," Wong said.

The company pitches itself to filmmakers, IP owners and exhibitors as a single partner covering both the production technology and the distribution needed to get interactive titles onto cinema screens. The Taiwan dates form part of a wider push across Asia, with releases in further international markets planned for 2027.

articles.title: Vin Diesel's Panned 24-Year-Old Attempt to Be James Bond Is About to Get Harder to Watch in December
articles.summary: Courtesy of Columbia Pictures Vin Diesel may be best know for his appearances in The Fast and Furious franchise, but he has spent many years attempting to kickstart other franchises that could have been just as big as his high-octane, star-studded street-racing-turned-space-travelling saga. One such movie was released in 2002, when Diesel attempted to muscle into the action spy […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Vin Diesel may be best know for his appearances in The Fast and Furious franchise , but he has spent many years attempting to kickstart other franchises that could have been just as big as his high-octane, star-studded street-racing-turned-space-travelling saga. One such movie was released in 2002, when Diesel attempted to muscle into the action spy genre and become a bigger, louder James Bond in his role as extreme-sports daredevil Xander Cage in xXx . While the movie did generate a couple of sequels - although Diesel only returned for one of them, the movie was not the great success it could have been and has often been called one of the actor's most incoherent and wildly over-the-top movies - which is quite a feat when glancing back through his catalog of acting roles. Now, those who do have a soft spot for Diesel's xXx have only a limited time left to watch it before it leaves Netflix on December 1.

In 2002, Diesel was coming off the success of The Fast and the Furious a year earlier, and a reteaming with that movie's director Rob Cohen seemed like the best route to another hit for the actor. The film follows Diesel's Xander Cage as he is recruited by Samuel L. Jackson's NSA handler Augustus Gibbons to infiltrate a dangerous group of Russian terrorists. Costarring Asia Argento and Marton Csokas, the film was billed as James Bond meets punk rock - even knowingly having a tuxedo-wearing spy killed off in its opening sequence to send a message - but after landing itself a 48% Rotten Tomatoes score, it became clear that the film was a very divisive affair. Even with renowned critic Roger Ebert surprisingly fighting its corner with a three and a half stars score and comment that "in its own punk way, xXx is as good as a good Bond movie," the film couldn't quite manage to please the majority.

Despite coming with a title that could cause many problems for search engine results, xXx is a film that probably deserved more attention and love than it received. Audiences were a little more onboard with the chaotic and frantic action flick, giving it a 58% Popcornmeter rating, with many recent reviews pointing out that while the movie may be "big and dumb," it is not the worst way to pass a couple of hours. Some call it "a pretty decent action movie if you don't mind the action being completely unbelievable," others call it "the worst movie I've ever seen." That kind of vastly differing opinion did not hurt the movie's box office performance as it turned a reasonable $80 million budget into a $277 million gross. That of course led to a sequel, xXx: State of the Union , in 2005, but this time it was Ice Cube in the driving seat with Diesel passing on a return.

In 2017, 15 years after his previous appearance, Diesel unexpectedly did return to the franchise in the blatantly titled, xXx: The Return of Xander Cage. Reviews of the movie were even more brutal than the original, but once again, coming in the wake of several huge Fast & Furious movies , Diesel's xXx comeback led to a $346 million worldwide haul, and although a fourth movie has been discussed , it has yet to really get any traction. While Diesel may have starred in other more popular movies, those looking to have a blast without thinking too hard about it could do worse than to track down xXx before it leaves Netflix on December 1.

Does xXx deserve more love? Would you come back for a second viewing if you have already seen it? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: David Fincher Reflects on Alien 3 After 34 Years, And Reveals The Original Pitch That Got Him the Job
articles.summary: Thirty-four years after the release of Alien 3, David Fincher still thinks the pitch that got him the job was a good one. The director isn't particularly receptive to praise from fans of the movie, but he's willing to talk about the movie he set out to make. Fincher envisioned a group of prisoners who […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Thirty-four years after the release of Alien 3 , David Fincher still thinks the pitch that got him the job was a good one. The director isn't particularly receptive to praise from fans of the movie, but he's willing to talk about the movie he set out to make. Fincher envisioned a group of prisoners who had been written off by society realizing that the one good thing they could do with their lives was make sure the Xenomorph died with them.

Much of that pitch actually made it into Alien 3 . What's particularly telling about Fincher's approach to the movie, though, is how much thought he'd given to the evolution of the franchise under Ridley Scott and James Cameron. Fincher saw a progression in what Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) was willing to risk her life for between the first two movies. He wanted to put Ripley in the company of men whose lives were considered expendable and explore what they would be willing to give their lives for. Speaking with Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , Fincher explained how he arrived at the pitch that sold Weaver and the producers on him directing the movie.

David Fincher Wanted Alien 3 to Be a Movie About Redemption Fincher considers the original Alien one of the 10 greatest movies ever made. He loves that Scott gets the audience to disagree with Ripley's decision not to let Kane, played by John Hurt, back aboard the Nostromo. The crew wants to save Kane's life, even though Ripley is the only person adhering to the protocol to keep everyone alive. As Fincher points out, 15 minutes later, we're all thinking, "We should have listened to the tall girl." Despite the considerable differences between Scott and Cameron's movies, Fincher sees a throughline in their treatment of Ripley. "The first movie is go back for the cat, and the second movie is go back for the child," explained Fincher. Ripley goes from risking her life for Jonesy in Alien to essentially becoming a mother again in Aliens .

Fincher's pitch for Alien 3 took into consideration how little regard the people in power in the Alien universe have for human life. If Weyland-Yutani was willing to sacrifice the crew of the Nostromo to get its hands on a Xenomorph, what chance did the inhabitants of a prison colony have? "We are all going to die tonight," Fincher said of the realization he wanted the prisoners to come to. "The only face-saving that we can do here is to take that thing with us."

Perhaps the best argument for Fincher's original pitch is the performance Charles S. Dutton gives in Alien 3 . Dillon has already devoted much of his life to seeking redemption through religion. Ripley's arrival on Fiorina 161 affords him and the other prisoners an opportunity to find it. The 2003 Assembly Cut of Alien 3 benefits considerably from the additional time we get to spend with these men before Ripley asks them to help her kill the creature. What makes Fincher's pitch such a good follow-up to the first two movies is that Ripley is now asking other people to make the kind of decision she's made twice before. Nobody would blame these men for wanting to get as far away from the creature as possible. They may well be the last people in the universe who owe humanity anything. And yet, they're the ones tasked with saving it.

Fincher may not like his own movie, but it has gained a considerable following from devoted fans like Christopher Nolan. Perhaps on your next watch, the film can hit a little different knowing what Fincher's ambitions were. Do you love Alien 3 ? Let us know what you think in the comments below.

articles.title: James Gunn's DC Exit Has People Asking About Keanu Reeves And Constantine Again (& I Don’t Hate It)
articles.summary: Does this mean Constantine could be coming back soon?
articles.content:
With James Gunn and Peter Safran’s exiting DC , it's unknown if the DCU will continue or if we can expect yet another reboot. However, with one chapter closing for the studio, the start of a new might mean some long-gestating projects could get a second chance. Amid the corporate change, people have been asking about Keanu Reeves ' long-discussed Constantine sequel again, and honestly, I don’t hate the possibility of seeing the 2005 movie finally get a follow-up.

This is sure to be music to some fans' ears amid the major corporate shift. Jeremy Latcham, a Marvel Studios alum who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy , is stepping into the role of DC Studios CEO. As a result, Gunn’s DC universe might be over , and Lawrence -- who's sympathetic to the exiting CEOs -- seems to be confident that this could open the door for a Constantine sequel.

2005's Constantine has earned quite the cult following. Believe it or not, Reeves wasn’t fans' first pick for the role, and that's because of how much of a departure from the comics his take on John is. The character has lived on in the live-action space since then, with Matt Ryan taking on the trench coat in 2014 for a short-lived NBC show. Ryan continued to portray Constantine in The CW’s Arrowverse and voiced the DC antihero in various animated works through 2024.

articles.title: DC Fans Can Save Years of Collecting With This Rare Swamp Thing Comic Lot
articles.summary: Sales for the original Swamp Thing may not have been strong, but the character has endured — incidentally turning those early issues into one of the most sought-after DC titles of its tumultuous Bronze Age. The Bronze Age was an era of growing pains for DC Comics, who were struggling to adapt to a changing […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Sales for the original Swamp Thing may not have been strong, but the character has endured — incidentally turning those early issues into one of the most sought-after DC titles of its tumultuous Bronze Age. The Bronze Age was an era of growing pains for DC Comics, who were struggling to adapt to a changing marketplace and increasingly stiff competition from Marvel. For readers, there was one clear benefit: the publisher understood themselves to be losing their grip on what was popular or appealing to its readers, and was willing to take risks. Editors let creatives push the comic book medium and the super-hero genre in new directions, and the result was some of the strangest, most exciting stories DC ever published. Jack Kirby's epic " Fourth World " saga emerged from this era, as did Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams' character-redefining Green Lantern / Green Arrow and Batman runs. However, few Bronze Age titles are as iconic or as sought-after as the original Len Wein and Bernie Wrightson issues of Swamp Thing .

Besides Kirby's aforementioned Fourth World titles ( The New Gods especially), few Bronze Age DC titles are as collectible as Swamp Thing 's first volume. Wrightson lent interiors and stunning covers to the first ten, while Wein scripted the first thirteen. This Heritage Auctions lot assembles the first twenty-one issues of Swamp Thing in a single lot, all in high-grade condition. The estimated value is listed by Heritage at around seven hundred and fifty dollars, but the real value of the lot is the time it saves the buyer. The lot includes all ten of the highly-sought after Bernie Wrightson-penciled issues, which usually necessitate years of patient collecting to assemble — as well as some hard questions about how much you're willing to pay and whether you're willing to compromise on condition.

Changing censorship standards in the early seventies allowed for horror comics — after being functionally banned for more than a decade — to make their return to newsstands. A generation of creators who had grown up on the controversial E.C. titles of the 1950s were entering the field, and were eager to lend their talents to the genre. Anthology titles like House of Mystery and House of Secrets were converted into horror books, and strong reader response supported an explosion of new horror titles like The Witching Hour, The Phantom Stranger , and The Demon . Swamp Thing was spun-off from a short story in House of Secrets #92, also by Wein and Wrightson. For the ongoing series, the duo retold the Southern gothic origin of the character, updating it for the modern era. While House of Secrets ' Alex Olsen became Swamp Thing because of a fire set by a romantic rival, Swamp Thing 's Alec Holland was killed for refusing to give over the secrets of his world-hunger ending bio-restorative formula to a shady criminal cabal. What didn't change was Wrightson's striking design for Swamp Thing, which resembles the artist's later interpretation of the Frankenstein Monster .

A more direct take on the Frankenstein Monster would come the following issue with the "Patchwork Man," a demented experiment by the mad Anton Arcane, who revives his brother Gregori from the dead after he's blown apart by a forgotten World War-era landmine. For Len Wein's initial thirteen issues especially, Swamp Thing existed in a dark, gothic world that — but for a team-up with Batman in Swamp Thing #7 — felt totally outside the DC Universe. It was a world of witches, eldritch horrors, and clockwork men, and every issue felt like it plunged Swamp Thing into a different nightmare out of Poe, Bierce, or Lovecraft. That was, however, Swamp Thing 's failing: Wein didn't know how to break Swamp Thing out of a "monster of the week" formula, and by the end of his thirteen-issue tenure, he felt the title was growing stale. The only real continuity thread was a Fugitive -esque subplot about Swamp Thing being pursued by federal agent Matt Cable, who mistakenly believes him responsible for Alec and Linda Holland's deaths. Subsequent writers David Michelinie and Gerry Conway had the same struggles, compounded by another mounting problem: waning reader interest.

The horror comic book explosion burned bright, but it did not burn for long. By the mid-seventies, titles like Tomb of Dracula , Werewolf by Night , and Swamp Thing were struggling to attract the strong readership of just a few years prior. Creators also found themselves burnt out, finding the storytelling potential of these character surprisingly limited. Swamp Thing 's final issues (by Gerry Conway, in collaboration with David Anthony Kraft for #24) attempted to revive the title by drastically changing its status quo: Alec Holland regains his humanity at the end of issue #23, and does not appear as Swamp Thing at all in the final issue. For the rest of the decade, Swamp Thing appeared only sporadically, serving as a supporting character to the Challengers of the Unknown (again written by Gerry Conway), as well as a guest star in team-up titles The Brave and the Bold and DC Comics Presents . The early issues were well-regarded by fans, but it wasn't enough to ensure a future — at least not until one of those fans bought the film rights.

Swamp Thing was a dormant character when entertainment lawyer, academic, and comic book geek Michael Uslan bought the film rights from DC. Uslan had been stymied by a years-long effort to get a darker, more grounded Batman film off the ground, and decided it would be easier to have creative control over a less well-known DC character. He chose Swamp Thing , feeling its stories and tone would be well-suited to adaptation. With Wes Craven in the director's chair, Uslan and business partner Benjamin Melniker set Swamp Thing for a 1982 release. To capitalize, DC decided to revive the Swamp Thing comic, launching Saga of the Swamp Thing at the same time as the film hit theaters. Saga of the Swamp Thing hit the same creative speed-bumps as its predecessor, and was due for cancellation by the time writer Martin Pasko left the series. Having little to lose by the decision, DC gave Saga of the Swamp Thing to a relative industry newcomer, British writer Alan Moore. Moore was told he could do as he liked with the title, given its precarious state.

The result was one of the most critically acclaimed comics ever published, turning Swamp Thing into one of DC's most popular characters among comic readers. Succeeded by penciller and co-plotter Rick Veitch, Moore's Swamp Thing brought complex, long-form storytelling to the character, taking it in strange directions in the process. Instead of a mutated Alec Holland, Swamp Thing was a plant that believed it was Alec Holland, the latest in a mystic line of "Guardians of the Green." This Swamp Thing was instrumental in the creation of DC's adult-oriented "Vertigo" imprint, as well as the gradual abandonment of the Comics Code Authority. It's perhaps best known for introducing John Constantine , routinely upheld alongside Swamp Thing as one of DC's best characters.

Although lauded for its experimentation and innovation, Moore and Veitch's Swamp Thing stayed rooted in the work of Wein and Wrightson, not only in using characters and ideas from the original run, but evoking its mood. Reprinted as The Roots of the Swamp Thing contemporaneously to Moore's ongoing, the first volume of Swamp Thing cemented itself as one of DC's most influential comics in the 1980s. It was at this time that those early issues took on their collectible status, which has only grown through the intervening decades as demand continues to outstrip supply. Both the Wein and the Moore runs of Swamp Thing have remained constantly in print since the rise of trade paperbacks and omnibuses, leaving new readers to discover their work every year. If they're lucky, it may be one such reader who wins the twenty-one issues of Swamp Thing on auction at Heritage, which planted the seed for the decades of Swamp Thing stories to follow.

What's your favorite Swamp Thing comic? Leave a comment below and join the conversation now in the ComicBook Forum !

articles.title: Marvel Studios Just Picked Fans Over Hollywood Prestige With One Massive Avengers: Doomsday Decision
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Marvel has chosen not to pre-screen Avengers: Doomsday for awards recognition. While Sony has been promoting Spider-Man: Brand New Day for the Oscars, Marvel is taking a strikingly different approach to Avengers: Doomsday. Although most studios want to push their movies for awards recognition, it seems that Marvel is looking to push its next movie […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Marvel has chosen not to pre-screen Avengers: Doomsday for awards recognition. While Sony has been promoting Spider-Man: Brand New Day for the Oscars, Marvel is taking a strikingly different approach to Avengers: Doomsday . Although most studios want to push their movies for awards recognition, it seems that Marvel is looking to push its next movie straight to the fans and not bother with the major guilds and critics associations who are watching this year's movies for the awards calendar.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe knows it has a winner in Avengers: Doomsday , and the movie will destroy box office records. It is already set to break the opening weekend box office total of Spider-Man: Brand New Day , which became the highest domestic box office in history. According to Variety , Marvel won't screen the movie in advance to critics or voting bodies to protect the closely guarded plot.

There are some fans who believe that Marvel has already revealed too many surprises for Avengers: Doomsday . With Chris Evans' return as Steve Rogers spotted in the trailers and the arrival of the original X-Men for what might be one of the last times, there is a lot that we already know about the movie. However, there are also likely big surprises that haven't been revealed yet, and Marvel wants to guard those secrets until the fans have a chance to see the movie. From Doctor Doom's actual role in the movie to some characters that Marvel is almost assuredly hiding, the studio isn't taking any chances with leaks.

Both awards bodies and critics groups often have deadlines in December to get in their votes for the year's best, and with Avengers: Doomsday getting a December 18 theatrical release, the timing will cut it very close for many of the awards. However, Marvel also knows that a lot of critics have an anti-superhero bias, so the awards might not be as important as keeping plot points a secret. Critics are also usually under an NDA when it comes to revealing anything that happens in the movie, but as history has shown, not all critics follow these rules.

Avengers: Doomsday is almost surely going to have big surprises , especially for people who are unfamiliar with the comic book story that the movie is based on. This is likely to be similar to Avengers: Infinity War , but it will be a long wait since there will be a year between Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars , just as Endgame came out a year after Avengers: Infinity War . However, while the movie won't be screened early for BAFTA, the Golden Globes, and other early awards groups, it will still have a chance for the Oscars, although it will be a little close to the deadlines for several categories.

What are your thoughts on Marvel passing on possible awards and focusing on fans instead? Let us know when you plan on seeing Avengers: Doomsday in the comments below.

articles.title: I Love Julie Bowen’s Mom-Coded Way Of Trolling Modern Family Co-Stars Ariel Winter And Nolan Gould
articles.summary: They better listen to their mother.
articles.content:
Modern Family may have ended, but Julie Bowen has never stopped being a "mom" to her on-screen kiddos. For instance, Bowen was present when TV daughter Sarah Hyland got married in 2022, and both were part of that epic cast reunion at her wedding . Of course, Bowen also has love for her other faux kids, Ariel Winter and Nolan Gould. In fact, Bowen gave them a shout out during a recent event, and she trolled them in a seriously mom-coded way that's hard not to love.

This is sitcom-level irony, but this kind of fun tends to happen amongst the cast. For instance, Winter has playfully called out on-screen big sis Hyland for having a mini reunion without sending an invite to her and Gould. However, Bowen's comments are particularly funny, because they speak to the jokey but somewhat maternal relationship she has with her young co-stars.

Not only are they NOT together, but it turns out that the best friend of your best friend makes for a good boyfriend. Winter is currently dating Gould’s best friend , after being introduced to him by her TV bro. Given she keeps her private life mostly out of public eye, she hasn’t revealed many details about the relationship. I'd imagine her former co-stars are update to date, though, as Bowen previously shared that their close bond is why the cast has remained on such friendly terms .

It's a moment like this that makes me wish a Modern Family revival of sorts would happen at some point. The cast's chemistry was just too perfect, and they clearly continue to have that bond off camera. I'm not sure whether ABC would be interested in such a production, but I'll keep my fingers crossed that it happens.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Throughout my childhood and into my adulthood, I have always loved building a team of Pokemon and completing the mainline game. Becoming Champion has been like a proof of my skill and friendship with my Pokemon. But after accomplishing this goal, there is essentially nothing left to do. Pokemon Gold and Silver and Emerald offer the best post-game content, but aside from these, the series has lacked real incentive to continue playing besides catching legendary Pokemon or completing the Pokedex. All it would take is one single change to make the postgame not only more engaging, but perhaps even better than the main playthrough.

Becoming champion seldom is a reward, because the postgame just has you battling the champion again. But what if it didn't? I'd love to see a Pokemon game that leaves your original character as the champion and then time skips, having you play the child of said champion beginning their own Pokemon journey for the first time. The region would have changed, familiar characters would have grown older, and an entirely new generation of trainers would be pursuing their dreams. Instead of exploring the region with an overpowered team, players would embark on another adventure shaped by everything they accomplished during the main story. It would give players a second Pokemon adventure within the same game but with greater emotional connection.

Pokemon Gold and Silver , or more specifically Crystal , remains my favorite game in the series because we return to Kanto after defeating the Elite Four. Revisiting familiar locations, collecting another eight badges, and eventually challenging Red at Mt. Silver is one of my favorite childhood memories . No game in the series has topped this, except obviously the remakes HeartGold and SoulSilver , but what made these games special wasn't necessarily the amount of content they offered, but how discovering what had happened to Kanto became an adventure in itself.

Pokemon games after this have experimented with different approaches to postgame content, sometimes with excellent results. However, battling increasingly powerful trainers or hunting Legendary Pokemon just doesn't compare. Pokemon games after this have experimented with different approaches to postgame content, sometimes with excellent results. However, battling increasingly powerful trainers or hunting Legendary Pokemon just doesn't compare.

A time skip would address this problem without requiring Game Freak to develop an entirely separate region. Players would choose another starter Pokemon, assemble a new team, and challenge the Pokemon League again. However, their knowledge of the region wouldn't necessarily help them. Familiar opponents could have different Pokemon, while previously difficult battles might disappear altogether. More importantly, players would have a reason to revisit every town and route beyond searching for items or completing their Pokedex.

Game Freak has already shown how effective revisiting a previous region is. Gold and Silver showed this first, but Pokemon Black and White 2 showed another example of this. Taking place two years after their predecessors, these sequels introduced new locations, Gym Leaders, and changes to Unova's Pokedex. Seeing Cheren become a Gym Leader and Bianca become Professor Juniper's assistant was particularly satisfying after spending so much time with them in Pokemon Black and White .

Entire towns could undergo renovations, while smaller communities could develop into bustling cities. Routes could change due to natural disasters, urban development, or Pokemon migration. A forest previously populated by Bug-type Pokemon might become home to Grass and Fairy-type Pokemon, while construction could attract Steel-type Pokemon elsewhere. Game Freak could even introduce new regional variants and evolutions, providing surprises for players who thought they knew everything about the region.

The biggest opportunity, however, would be seeing what happened to the characters players met throughout their original adventure. Former rivals could become members of the Elite Four, Gym Leaders could retire, and their children could become the next generation of Pokemon trainers. Even minor characters could return in unexpected roles. These changes would make the Pokemon world feel alive rather than existing in a perpetual state of stagnation once players become Champion.

I've always found battling Red at Mt. Silver exciting, not just because he is one of the strongest trainers in a mainline game, but because of the connection players have with the character. He represents the player character from Pokemon Red and Blue . Imagine experiencing that same feeling with a trainer whose appearance, name, and Pokemon team you selected yourself. Game Freak could record the player's original Hall of Fame team and use it when designing the final Champion battle.

There is also an opportunity to tell a more mature Pokemon story about expectations and family. Playing as the child of the reigning Pokemon Champion would naturally introduce pressure to live up to their parent's accomplishments. Other trainers might question whether your success comes from talent or privilege. Your new character could struggle to establish their own identity, especially when encountering people who remember their parent's adventure.

Naturally, players should retain access to their original trainer and Pokemon collection through a character-switching feature. Nobody should lose hundreds of hours of progress simply to experience the postgame. However, restricting the new protagonist's access to that collection until they become Champion would preserve the challenge. Pokemon has spent decades encouraging players to become the very best, but it rarely explores what happens afterward. I'd love to see an adventure that explores the legacy of your accomplishments and truly challenges you to top them.

articles.summary: James Bond clearly hasn't met Christopher Nolan.
articles.content:
When we think of secrecy surrounding movies, naturally we think MCU, but the amount of secrecy that went into The Odyssey is insane. While I knew everything about it was kept under wraps, I didn’t realize just how much until I heard John Leguizamo ’s story about landing the script, and it’s WILD.

Leguizamo’s performance as Eumaeus has been called “sublime” by critics , and it’s easy to see why Nolan thought he was the right fit. Though the actor understands there’s a certain scene in the movie that earned him some hate for “the rest of cinema history,” and if you’ve seen it, then you know what he’s referring to. The actor didn’t even know the extent of his part until he got the script, which came to him as a top secret mission fit for James Bond :

Perhaps Marvel needs to take some notes from Nolan. While this seems like an insane level of secrecy for a book to screen adaptation , I admire the commitment to "no spoilers." Though the journalist asked the most important question, who delivered the script? Surely, FedEx wasn’t tasked with such a feat. Turns out one of Nolan’s personal assistants hand delivered it. However, there was still another step for him to be able to keep the confidential script:

The cloak and dagger seems to have worked as not even Tom Holland seems to have leaked anything. Additionally, Leguizamo shared that whenever Nolan made tweaks , the actor would have to turn in the old pages. articles.title: This Poison Ivy Figure From Batman: The Animated Series Has Something Most Other Prototypes Don't
articles.summary: The various art styles used in Batman comics are almost as iconic as the Dark Knight himself. From Frank Miller's grizzled and hulking version to Jim Lee's clean and detailed linework, we've seen many memorable adaptations over the years. But I think we can all agree that the most beloved art style belongs to Batman: […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The various art styles used in Batman comics are almost as iconic as the Dark Knight himself. From Frank Miller's grizzled and hulking version to Jim Lee's clean and detailed linework, we've seen many memorable adaptations over the years. But I think we can all agree that the most beloved art style belongs to Batman: The Animated Series . The future-noire version of Gotham gave us many iconic character depictions, but this prototype of Hasbro's Poison Ivy action figure might just be better than the final version. The first thing that stands out about it is that unlike most prototypes, this one is fully painted. While prototypes usually stick to the color of the base mold, this one features the character's iconic green and red. However, that's not where the differences end.

As compared to the final version Hasbro put out, this prototype actually manages to capture Poison Ivy's trademark sensuality. Firstly, the overall mold appears to be taller and more slender, while her green leggings are missing, making it appear like she's wearing a one-piece swimsuit. While this is a diversion from the original version of the character, the manufacturer may have perhaps walked back the idea as they figured it would be a bit too much for kids. Apart from that, her red hair features a completely different mold, along with the detailing on her face. The difference on the facial features is most stark, with this prototype featuring sharp and detailed features that make the final figure's look like a cheap knockoff version of it.

Other differences include the color of Ivy's lipstick and eyebrows, along with the prototype wearing heels instead of flat shoes. It's evident that Hasbro had a great prototype on hand but put out a much inferior looking final product. There could be many reasons for this, like production costs, timelines, or the fact that it looked a little too risqué for kids. The result was an unfortunate looking figure that took away from one of Ivy's most recognizable traits, her beauty. It's truly unfortunate when brilliantly designed prototypes are cut down to inferior final products, and this Ivy figure shows just how much things can change from the design phase to production.

A noteworthy feature of this particular prototype is that it is colored, unlike most others I've seen. While this is a bit of an assumption, it could mean that Hasbro changed its mind at the last possible minute, before the figure went into mass production. Prototypes are usually created for every stage, including mold, painting, and packaging, so this figure being painted implies that it may have passed the initial mold prototyping phase. Of course, we'll never really know what went on behind the scenes, and how this stunning prototype became the comparatively poor final figure we saw on shelves. It's evident that fans of Batman: The Animated Series appreciate the work and detailing that went into this prototype, or else they wouldn't be willing to pay over $380 dollars for it.

Who is your favorite character from Batman: The Animated Series? Let us know in the comments.

Former Netflix executive Bela Bajaria put the emphasis on her belief in the transformative the power of storytelling in accepting the Founders Award Monday night at the International Emmy Awards in New York.

Bajaria was ousted from her role as chief content officer of Netflix in a very public fashion last month amid a larger shake-up of content leadership at the streaming giant. In her speech, her first major public appearance since her departure, Bajaria reflected on her career journey to the top echelon of Hollywood as a senior executive at CBS and Universal Television prior to joining Netflix in 2016. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Cannes Condemns Five-Year Prison Sentence Against Iranian Palme d’Or Winner Jafar Panahi and Pleads for International Support

In a nod to the Thanksgiving holiday this week, Bajaria opened by expressing her gratitude for the opportunities she's been afforded since her family relocated to Southern California in the late 1970s when she was in grade school.

“Gratitude isn’t passive or soft. It’s earned. Gratitude is strength in knowing nothing is guaranteed and nothing can be taken for granted. Gratitude is the appreciation for both struggle and success, and sharing the journey with others,” Bajaria told the crowd.

During most of the past decade, Bajaria was focused on building out Netflix's local-language TV content operation at a scale never before seen in the industry. The experience was profound as the regional teams set off on a search for new creative voices.

“Whether I was in Mumbai or Madrid, Bangkok or Berlin or anywhere in between — there’s nothing like being on the ground finding that original voice — in their homes, or sharing a meal, and looking eye to eye with openness, curiosity and respect,” Bajaria said. “I’ve seen firsthand how the saying is true: to paraphrase, you can ‘travel the world and never be a stranger.' ” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“I’m full of gratitude for how far that idea — that belief — has forever transformed storytelling all over the world and not just in entertainment but in sports, brands and fandoms of all kinds,” she said. “Gratitude to all of you — you tell your stories from your own country and in your own language. Someone far away, who you will never meet, will watch and remember your work in the most unexpected ways. You will stay with them forever.”

Bajaria's kudo was presented by Keri Russell, star of Netflix's “The Diplomat” and was preceded by a video with compliments on her leadership and creative instincts from such notable stars and creatives as Kate Hudson, Hasan Minhaj, Peter Morgan, Lee Sung Jin, Shonda Rhimes, Tan France, Ricardo Darín, Alex Pina, David Beckham and Hwang Dong-hyuk.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google One of 2028's biggest upcoming games — currently only confirmed for PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X — is coming to Nintendo Switch 2 when it releases. This has not been confirmed, but it may have just been leaked. The new leak comes from Amazon, and specifically, Amazon News, and has since been deleted by Amazon, but not before the Internet got its receipt.

Back on December 11, 2025, Tomb Raider: Catalyst was announced at The Game Awards by series developer Crystal Dynamics and Amazon Games. Now, a year later, Amazon News officially noted the game was coming to Nintendo Switch 2, and seems to suggest this version would be available at launch. This could just be an honest error, but the timing is interesting, because The Game Awards are right around the corner, and it would be fitting for the game to reappear with a new trailer and word of a new platform. In other words, this may be less of an honest error and simply letting the beans spill a little early, which happens. Many ports, release dates, and even games themselves have leaked this way in the past.

A Nintendo Switch 2 port for the game seems completely plausible if not likely, but often Nintendo gets ports of games after their launch. If this version is leaking this early, it's reasonable to assume the Nintendo Switch 2 version will be ready at launch. That said, take everything here with a grain of salt. None of this is official information. For what it is worth, neither Crystal Dynamics nor Amazon Games have commented on the potential leak. If it were fake, they could have just shut it down, but to be fair, many game developers and publishers have a universal policy of silence when it comes to rumors, leaks, and specualtion.

The 14th Tomb Raider Game For those who do not know what Tomb Raider: Catalyst is, it is the 14th installment in the series, at least of the mainline variety. It's not another reboot, though. Rather, it is a sequel to Tomb Raider: Underworld , released in 2008. To this end, the story takes place in Northern India after the events of Underworld , where Lara Croft must navigate the aftermath of a mythical cataclysm. While a sequel to Underworld , the expectation is that the game is going to be made in a way that playing Underworld won't be required. Meanwhile, the new installment looks poised to make a huge change to the series .

Officially, Tomb Raider: Catalyst is in development for PC, PS5, Xbox Series S, and Xbox Series X. Unofficially, it may be coming to Nintendo Switch 2 as well. Whatever the case, it is currently slated for release in 2027.

articles.title: Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?
articles.summary: After word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music's biggest superstar, there was some anticipation that Monday might turn out to be a bad day for Taylor Swift. Instead, it was just a bad day for journalism. As attention-seeking magazine articles […]
articles.content:
After word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music's biggest superstar, there was some anticipation that Monday might turn out to be a bad day for Taylor Swift . Instead, it was just a bad day for journalism. As attention-seeking magazine articles go, it's hard to remember one that landed with quite such an unanticipated — but very loud — thud as "The Mastermind," which has even hardened anti-Swifties wondering whether May Jeong slipped it through without editorial oversight, sneaking an alleged year's worth of work onto the internet in the dead of morning.

The alternative scenario was unthinkable. You would have to imagine that the author had actually been encouraged by editors to puzzle readers with a reported op-ed in which the subject of the piece — apparently, some top-tier celebrity! — is never named, yet still is subject to accusations that she picks her own friends, harbors ambitions, owned three pairs of Ugg boots while posing as a teenage commoner, and, most slanderously, was actually popular in school.

When was the last time a high-profile magazine piece got ratio-ed this badly? That would have been one year and one week ago, when an exclusive excerpt from Olivia Nuzzi's memoir, "American Canto," was released to an incredulous world. And if there's something that feels a little bit familiar about Jeong's oddball tactic of not naming names in her piece (or at least not the big ones), it's because this "you know who it's about, but we're not gonna say anyway" technique was a weird conceit last grafted into big-time American journalism by Nuzzi. That author referred to RFK only as "the Politician," her ex-boyfriend as "the man I did not marry," and so on. Nuzzi walked so that Jeong could run. Although this new piece is not any kind of roman a clef, she still feels compelled to euphemize Swift as "The Star," her former label as "The Machine," Scooter Braun as "The Manager," Charli xcx as "The Brat" and even a secondary source as "The Person Familiar."

You would think Vanity Fair's editors would recall the horrible reviews Nuzzi got for employing this gambit in "American Canto," especially since the excerpt that introduced that annoying running gag to the world was published in… Vanity Fair. (How quickly they forget, but monthly journalism is a grind.)

The article aims to unload secrets, but the secret we really need revealed is: Why do that? An interview with Jeoing is in order. Or perhaps she is saving the rationale for her journalism class at Princeton, which may be the only one destined to have "The Mastermind" as ciriculum. On first blush, a journalism non-pro might imagine that it was done to skirt libel laws, although that explanation holds no water, since the writer does quote several of her lowest-level sources by name, like the kids from Swift's school who are ready to call her out now for not having been friendless or unmoneyed. (The former classmates will pick up some notoriety now, but will they regret that they could have become even more legendary if they'd been ID-ed as "The Girl Who Noticed The Star's Uggs"?) No, it seems more likely that Jeong did it because we are, all of us, just archetypes in a fable. Except for the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High, who is un-archetypical enough to require a first and last name. Related Stories Cannes Condemns Five-Year Prison Sentence Against Iranian Palme d’Or Winner Jafar Panahi and Pleads for International Support

Or perhaps Jeong refrains from naming Swift because she is the female equivalent of two other characters who are often referred to as He Who Must Not Be Named: Voldemort and Trump. Certainly the article seems to see Swift as an exemplor of the banality of evil, or, more to the point, a modern-day, real-life Regina George from "Mean Girls." (No, not making that up, the journalist really goes with that.) Nearly every sentence is intended as a slap. Most journos writing a piece remotely in this vein — a reported one, as opposed to a straight opinion — would try to leaven it at least once or twice with a positive or just neutral observation, before dropping the next bomb. "The Mastermind," to its honest credit, dispenses with any "See, I went into this with an open mind" niceties. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The Star is found to be "making herself a metonym for all women, successfully equat(ing) criticism against her as criticism against womenkind." Compared to Katy Perry (or "The California Girl"), who is "an adult pretending to be a child," Swift "might be a child pretending to be an adult." She "has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood." For Swift, "all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism." And then from there, Jeoing gets to some of Swift's bad qualities. (Just kidding.)

If this were framed in any way as a commentary, as opposed to Vanity Fair objectively speaking in the voice of God, it wouldn't catch much notice. But instead, the magazine frames it as an ultimate profile, the result of a year of work and talking to "over 100 sources." We have to take the editors' word for that, because the reportage, as printed, only quotes six sources on the record: the mother of a man who directed Swift in her school plays, a guitar teacher, a school music teacher, two girls who sat near Swift in music class, and a poet who is called in to assess how lyrics work. Five others are quoted anonymously: someone who used to be close to Swift called The Person Familiar; a music pro called The Exec; a mystery collaborator with a profession that must be kept secret; a musician who toured with Swift; and a critic who was ostracized after slamming her. Now, reporters do often get great background information from interviews they don't quote, so the 100-plus figure doesn't sound unrealistic. But if these dozen or so sources were the best that the story had to actually quote — including a poet and a critic — you do have to wonder who the other 85-plus were, to be less quotable. (An editor's introduction to the piece says one of the people interviewed was a "lover" of Swift's, but we'll just have to guess if the writer got to Joe Alwyn.) blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

All that said, there are a handful of interesting questions and critical observations scattered through Jeong's piece. (See? This is the part where you throw in something nice, to show you were objective.) If you removed the promise of fact-finding and this existed as an essay on Salon — RIP — you could credit her with some food-for-thought lines and decently snarky zingers. (Sure, I chuckled when Jeong, alluding to Travis Kelce, wrote, "Regretfully we must call him Redwood.")

But the veneer of investigative reporting placed upon this piece mostly shows just how low the bar is for an attempted expose anymore. Even without the terminally cutesy names. It'd be nice to suppose that Jeong really did come up with something after a year — there is so much hinted at that is quickly dropped — and that Vanity Fair's lawyers gutted the piece to within an inch of a life. But more probably it's an example of snark masquerading as reportage. And it's a lesson that some journalists (even journalists that teach at Princeton) are too quick to succumb to a sad maxim, when an expensive and exhaustive fishing expedition doesn't turn up much: If you can't get the goods, just get cute. But don't expect readers who expect more out of their hit squads not to notice.

That was over four years ago in the heat of the pair figuring out the post-split situation . However, these days, the two seem to be on better terms. To that point, Sudeikis is even crediting his ex for the creation of his massively successful TV show, Ted Lasso (which just got big news by the way).

As Sudeikis shared during an interview at a special live edition of the show at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles, Wilde was the person who actually followed up with her then-partner on the Ted Lasso idea years before him and the other creators knew what to do with the character. As Sudeikis continued:

Wild, right? Mr. Ted Lasso himself, alongside two of his co-creators Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly, sat on the idea for a while until one day they were overflowing with ideas. And then, they sat on it again until this happened. In Sudeikis’ words:

Now that Ted Lasso is one of the best shows to watch with an Apple TV subscription , it’s pretty crazy to think how long the whole process took. It took so long that when the idea was first formed Sudeikis and Wilde went from being an engaged couple to splitting up . Thankfully it did, because it’s one of my favorite shows on streaming in recent years.

Former Netflix chief content officer Bela Bajaria addressed her exit from the streamer in her first public comments since her abrupt departure last month.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the 2026 International Emmys , where she's set to be honored with the Founders Award , Bajaria called her decade at Netflix "such an amazing, fun chapter" and shared she was "proud of so many of the things" that she and her team had accomplished.

"I'm excited about what's next, and I think this time is good for a little rest after a lot of global travel," she told THR on the red carpet ahead of the awards show, adding that she's "really open" to whatever the future holds.

Bajaria was ousted from her role at Netflix on Oct. 15, with former Fox and Disney exec Peter Rice taking her place as chief content officer.

Bajaria, who joined Netflix after serving as president of Universal Television at NBCUniversal, left the streamer as it shed 1,000 employees, roughly six percent of its workforce, including execs Doug Belgrad and, days after news broke of Bajaria leaving, film boss Dan Lin. Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick, the man behind Grand Theft Auto VI , is among the first raft of speakers confirmed for next year's SXSW London .

The conference is set to return to Shoreditch, east London, for its third year from May 24-29, where Zelnick will take to the stage to talk about building one of the world's biggest entertainment franchises (sales for the latest release have already out-grossed Christopher Nolan's box office behemoth The Odyssey ).

The upcoming installment is built around the theme "The Power of Human Potential," described by organizers as a deliberate focus on people in a year dominated by what machines can do. articles.title: Netflix Is About to Lose All Five Seasons of a Near-Perfect "Game of Thrones with Vikings" Series but You Still Have Time to Binge-Watch It
articles.summary: Courtesy of Netflix/Carnival Films & Television Everyone loves a big action-packed historical TV series and one show that could give Game of Thrones a run for its money is one of the best out there. However, the series that launched in 2015 and ran for five seasons and a wrap-up movie is about to become much harder to watch in the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Everyone loves a big action-packed historical TV series and one show that could give Game of Thrones a run for its money is one of the best out there. However, the series that launched in 2015 and ran for five seasons and a wrap-up movie is about to become much harder to watch in the U.S. as all episodes will be leaving its home on Netflix in less than a month. Yet all is not lost as you could easily binge the 46 episodes of The Last Kingdom before December 9 to see why this show has a massive 95% Popcornmeter rating on Rotten Tomatoes. The series' departure from Netflix has come as a surprise to fans, who assumed that as Netflix is co-producer they would be keeping the show on their platform permanently. However, with the show originally airing on BBC America before Netflix became involved it seems that pesky licensing rules are shipping it off the platform.

The Last Kingdom earned rave reviews from its first episodes and, unlike Game of Thrones , continued to please viewers through until its final episode. Based on the novels of Bernard Cornwell's The Saxon Stories series, the show is packed with brutal and bloody battles, political manipulation, and the kind of drama that made George R.R. Martin's fantasy epic such a hit on HBO. However, The Last Kingdom has its story rooted in real history. Even though Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire bases several aspects of its story in historical places and events, such as The Wall being a representation of Hadrian's Wall in northern England, and the battle of the Starks and Lannisters drawing inspiration from the War of the Roses between the houses of Lancaster and York, Cornwell's work is truer to the kind of power struggles that actually took place in England.

The Last Kingdom tells of the bloody struggle to reunite England during the ninth and 10th centuries. Dane raised Saxon Uhtred of Bebbanburg, played by Alexander Dreymon, is the central conflicted character of the saga, who fights to reclaim his ancestral home while struggling to work out which side he should actually be fighting for. Across five seasons, Uhtred's path is one that brings him into several intense conflicts, puts his loyalties to the test, and provides a thrilling story that kept both audiences and critics watching the show to its conclusion. Before the end of the series in 2022, a sequel feature length movie was announced under the title of The Last Kingdom: Seven Kings Must Die . The movie debuted on Netflix in 2023 to conclude the story.

The biggest achievement of The Last Kingdom was being able to maintain its high standard throughout the entire series. Game of Thrones proved how hard it can be to deliver a satisfying conclusion to a long-running series, but one thing the show had going for it was that all of its books were available at the time it reached the end. Where HBO's series needed to go beyond Martin's books in order to complete the tale, The Last Kingdom clearly benefited from having everything laid out ready in advance. That means that even if you have already seen it, The Last Kingdom is a series that is always worth a rewatch . If you live in the U.S., then you have until December 9 to get in on the action, which those in the U.K., Europe, and other territories, the series is set to remain with the streamer until 2028. The Last Kingdom: Seven Kings Must Die will not be leaving Netflix and will remain on the platform worldwide.

Have you see The Last Kingdom ? Is it better than Game of Thrones ? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

articles.title: Unannounced Doomsday Hero Has Been Hiding Their Casting in Plain Sight for Weeks, According to MCU Theory & The Reveal Will Be Amazing
articles.summary: Marvel fans think they've figured out how the studio plans to announce Iman Vellani's return as Ms. Marvel in Avengers: Doomsday. The actress has spent the last few months co-hosting Marvel's Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday podcast with Frank Alvarez. While Vellani's involvement in the movie has yet to be confirmed, the recent announcement that Hailee […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Marvel fans think they've figured out how the studio plans to announce Iman Vellani's return as Ms. Marvel in Avengers: Doomsday . The actress has spent the last few months co-hosting Marvel's Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday podcast with Frank Alvarez. While Vellani's involvement in the movie has yet to be confirmed, the recent announcement that Hailee Steinfeld will return as Kate Bishop has fans taking a closer look at the podcast's set. Specifically, they're looking at Vellani's chair.

Marvel Studios has managed to turn a piece of furniture into one of the most effective marketing tools in Hollywood. Since the hours-long livestream announcing the cast of Avengers: Doomsday , getting a chair has become a rite of passage for actors joining the movie. When Steinfeld received her chair while promoting Disney's Hexed , fans realized Vellani had been sitting in a similar director's chair since the podcast debuted in August. Fans on Reddit are now speculating that Marvel is saving the reveal of what's on the back of Vellani's chair for the final episode of the podcast.

Me, conspicuously eyeing the Iman Vellani chair on the Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday podcast. https://t.co/tjk5ozutHj pic.twitter.com/63PeuHFBCb

If Marvel wanted to sneak another casting announcement past fans, Vellani would be the perfect accomplice. The actress is arguably as big a Marvel fan as anyone watching the podcast. Getting to spend a few months talking about the MCU without letting slip that she's in the next Avengers movie seems like something Vellani would have a lot of fun with. This isn't the first time someone has potentially let slip that Vellani is in the movie, either. Earlier this year, Andy Serkis told Vellani he was excited to see her in Avengers: Doomsday . Whether Serkis knew something we didn't or was simply having some fun with the actress remains to be seen.

When we last saw Kamala Khan, she was doing her best Nick Fury impression. The post-credits scene of The Marvels saw Kamala show up at Kate Bishop's apartment to recruit the young archer. She even mentioned that Ant-Man had a daughter. Three years later, Marvel has confirmed that both Steinfeld and Kathryn Newton will appear in Avengers: Doomsday , but not the actress whose character was responsible for getting the team together in the first place. Adding to the speculation is footage from the ScreenX presentation of an Avengers: Doomsday trailer that appears to place Scott and Cassie Lang inside Kate's apartment. Could we finally be getting a payoff to the scene that closed out The Marvels ?

Vellani's absence from the original cast announcement was particularly surprising given how much of Kamala's story has revolved around her love of the Avengers and a piece of alien tech in her gauntlets. We were introduced to the character in an episode of Ms. Marvel that took her to AvengerCon. Getting to see Kamala interact with some of the heroes she grew up idolizing would be one of the joys of bringing her into an Avengers movie. For all the talk of returning X-Men and Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, Avengers: Doomsday also has an opportunity to make good on some of the promises Marvel made during the Multiverse Saga. It would be a shame to finally get the Young Avengers together without Kamala. Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on December 18th.

articles.title: 5 Marvel Characters Who Are Nothing Like Their Debut Appearances
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Comics Marvel Comics has changed a lot since the company started making superhero comics. However, while most heroes and villains change a lot over the years, they are still recognizable today compared to how they looked when they debuted. No matter how much Hulk has changed, he eventually goes back to how fans recognize him best. […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Marvel Comics has changed a lot since the company started making superhero comics. However, while most heroes and villains change a lot over the years, they are still recognizable today compared to how they looked when they debuted. No matter how much Hulk has changed, he eventually goes back to how fans recognize him best. Peter Parker might have grown up, but Spider-Man is still the same wisecracking hero he has always been. Even Magneto, who has been a hero for a very long time now, still has the same basic look and powers that he has had since he debuted in X-Men #1 (1963) so many years ago.

However, there are some heroes who debuted in Marvel Comics, and today they have changed drastically. In some cases, they have been de-aged, and in others they have developed deeper stories that made them so much more than what they originally were. There is also one hero who looks and acts the exact same, but her powers and origin have drastically changed thanks to an MCU streaming series.

Natasha Romanoff debuted in Tales of Suspense #52 (1964) by Stan Lee, Don Rico, and Don Heck. She was a Soviet agent sent to seduce Tony Stark while her partner Boris Turgenov attacked Anton Vanko and stole his armor. She had no costume, no red hair, and never threw a punch. She was infatuated with Stark's looks and wealth and easily distracted by jewelry, and she feared her Soviet superiors more than her enemies. She was a femme fatale who was used to distract and even assassinate wealthy and powerful men.

However, that is not how Black Widow looks or acts today. Once she defected, she eventually joined the Avengers and became a spy and secret agent working for the United States. The black suit and red hair debuted in The Amazing Spider-Man #86 (1970), and she ended up teaming with Daredevil starting in Daredevil #81, which is where her personality began to really change. Later stories rebuilt her origin around the Red Room, which implanted false memories, and that version morphed into the Black Widow fans know today.

Sam Wilson debuted in Captain America #117 (1969) by Stan Lee and Gene Colan. He is an interesting case because he has drastically changed not only in his role as a hero but also in his secret identity role. When Sam debuted, he was a social worker who helped the kids on the streets. He became the Falcon, a sidekick to Captain America, and they shared an interesting dynamic as Cap signified fighting for his country while Falcon was more about helping the people the country often ignored or forgot about.

Sam Wilson became Captain America in Captain America #25 (2014) after Steve Rogers lost the Super Soldier Serum and aged. He is still someone who fights more for the people than for the government. An example is when he fought against the anti-immigrant Sons of the Serpent on the U.S.-Mexico border, a storyline that made real-world news about the issues he faced in the comics. Sam returned to his Falcon role for a short time, but that part of his life is over with, and Sam is now as much Captain America as Steve Rogers is.

When Kamala Khan debuted, she was an Inhuman with the power to stretch and alter her body, similar to that of Plastic Man in DC Comics. She was also a teenager, and while she was a member of the Avengers for a time, she made her name as a leader on the teenage Champions team with Nova and Miles Morales. As a young, teenage Muslim hero, she was fresh and different, and she gave a new generation of fans a hero they could see themselves in.

However, things changed in comics for Kamala. While she is still the teenager who loves her family and has an intense fangirl attitude toward Captain Marvel, Kamala Khan is now a mutant/Inhuman hybrid . Marvel has said it always wanted her to be a mutant but made her an Inhuman because she debuted during a time when Marvel was emphasizing Inhumans over mutants for a period. This change happened after Kamala's death, when she ended up resurrected on Krakoa, with Professor X saying she had the latent X-gene. This also gave her new powers of creating hard light constructs, which debuted in her Disney+ MCU series.

Most fans know the Guardians of the Galaxy from the MCU movies, but that team is nothing like the original Guardians. The Guardians of the Galaxy from the movies debuted in 2008 during the Annihilation: Conquest miniseries . However, the original Guardians of the Galaxy debuted in Marvel Super-Heroes #18 (1968) by Arnold Drake, Gene Colan, and Roy Thomas. The first lineup was Vance Astro, Martinex, Charlie-27, and Yondu, each apparently the last of their kind, uniting against the alien Badoon in the 31st century.

This was also a team that played a big role in Marvel in the 1970s. They appeared in Giant-Size Defenders #5 and The Defenders #26-29 (1975), and they also had run-ins with the Avengers during that era. Tom DeFalco relaunched them in 1990 to capitalize on Star Trek: The Next Generation . In 2008, Marvel reimagined them as a team fighting in cosmic wars, with a lineup including Star-Lord, Rocket Raccoon, Groot, Gamora, Drax, Adam Warlock, Phyla-Vell, and Mantis.

Agatha Harkness debuted in Fantastic Four #94 (1969) by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. She was a woman who Reed Richards and Sue Richards hired as a child-rearing specialist for their baby Franklin. She was an elderly woman with gray hair, and Ben Grimm often jokingly called her an "old cow." She lived in a creepy old house on Whisper Hill, and she often joked that people thought she was a witch. In actuality, she was a witch. She ended up mentoring the Scarlet Witch and is the one who wiped the twins from Wanda's mind after they disappeared in West Coast Avengers.

That was her downfall as well, since Wanda found and killed her in "Avengers Disassembled," which is where the changes began. She later haunted Wanda as a ghost until Natalya Maximoff sacrificed herself to resurrect he r in Scarlet Witch #14. When Agatha came back, she was no longer an elderly woman and was now much younger, and she continued to clash with Wanda. The change made it easier for the MCU to make its version younger, with the character played by Kathryn Hahn.

Which characters do you think have had the better transformation over the years? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

articles.title: Did Marvel Edit Characters Out of the Avengers: Doomsday Trailer? Marvel Fans Spot Mystery Moments
articles.summary: Marvel Studios Avengers: Doomsday's final trailer was exactly what a lot of Marvel Cinematic Universe fans needed to see: a story that had heart and massive stakes to go along with all the Marvel characters that are going to cross over with one another for the first time, combining over a quarter-century of Marvel movie history into […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avengers: Doomsday 's final trailer was exactly what a lot of Marvel Cinematic Universe fans needed to see: a story that had heart and massive stakes to go along with all the Marvel characters that are going to cross over with one another for the first time, combining over a quarter-century of Marvel movie history into one film. However, all that new footage from Doomsday is also raising some very important new questions. And the Marvel fandom is putting their detective skills together to find some answers.

One of the biggest things being looked at right now is whether or not Marvel Studios is once again pulling a trick with the Avengers: Doomsday footage being shown in trailers. And, unlike ten years ago when we were all being fooled by the very first teasers for Avengers: Infinity War , now we know how to look at what's being shown to us a little bit closer, and with much more scrutiny.

A lot of MCU fans and bloggers have been dissecting the Avengers: Doomsday footage and picking up on the familiar pattern of scenes that have awkwardly conspicuous spaces left open in the frame. It suggests that digital editing has been used to remove a character (or characters ) from the actual finished shot, or that shots may not be entirely genuine at all.

Some key scenes from the latest trailer that seem odd include the shots of the Fantastic Four meeting with Steve Rogers in the 1950s, and later bringing him to Avengers Tower, all of which seem to be missing a character (or more) in the ensemble. Then there's the callback circular shot of the Avengers and X-Men assembling to battle Doom's Sentinels, where there is also space both in the center of the group and next to Sam Wilson (on his left!) where more characters are likely to appear.

Previous trailers also brought up the pivotal meeting scene between Wakanda and the Fantastic Four and Avengers, which has already revealed more visual effects not seen before, like water being displaced so that Namor and the undersea kingdom of Talokan (who we still don't see in the footage) can presumably join the alliance. So this isn't fan conspiracy: Marvel is changing the Avengers: Doomsday footage right in front of our eyes, just like it has before with so many other films.

Fans started catching on as far back as Spider-Man: Homecoming with its faux trailer scenes of Spider-Man and Iron Man flying/swinging into action together; Avengers: Infinity War was the biggest culprit, with Marvel Studios' digital wizards cooking up an entirely fake "Avengers Assemble" team charge during the Battle of Wakanda, featuring Hulk, who never even appeared again after the opening scenes! By the time Avengers: Endgame 's trailer was released, fans were savvy enough to see many of the "spaces" where missing characters were being hidden, while questioning whether other shots were real at all.

As for who Marvel Studios is hiding: ( POTENTIAL SPOILERS !)

One major fan theory says that it is actually Doom who is being edited out of the scenes between Steve Rogers and the Fantastic Four. It's long been rumored that Fantastic Four: First Steps ' post-credits scene of Doom meeting Franklin Richards will segue into Doom teaming up with Marvel's First Family , under the guise of saving the multiverse, while really scheming to create his own new reality.

Doom would supposedly help the F4 track the source of the multiverse collapse back to Steve and his altered timeline, living with Peggy Carter and his son, and use Steve to recruit the Avengers to pit that team against the X-Men and their world. Marvel would obviously want to hide that story detail because it raises so many other questions and theories they'd rather just let the movie answer for itself (like does Doom use Tony Stark's likeness to manipulate Steve – another secret worth hiding).

Shots like the Avengers and X-Men vs. the Sentinels could be hiding any number of characters . Some good guesses are that Monica Rambeau (Teyonah Parris) is involved in this, as an Earth-616 superhero who has been in the custody of the X-Men since she got portaled to Earth-10005 at the end of The Marvels . Other theories say that Ryan Reynolds' Deadpool and Hugh Jackman's Wolverine are part of this battle, but are being saved as a reveal in the film; some deeper fan theories state that characters like Bob/The Sentry/The Void (Lewis Pullman) will be more pivotal than we think, and will fight alongside his buddy and confidant Yelena Belova (Florence Pugh) when she goes to Earth-10005.

Either way, it's fun to know that Avengers: Doomsday is still holding back some big surprises for fans to discover in the theater. We'll soon find out when it's released on December 18th.

articles.title: I Knew Blade Runner 2099 Reviews Would Praise The Visuals, But I’m Surprised By Critics’ Big Critique
articles.summary: Well, I didn't see this coming.
articles.content:
Blade Runner 2099 has arguably been one of the most anticipated titles on the 2026 TV schedule , and there’s a good reason for that. Not only does it expand upon the classic science-fiction franchise, but it also has two capable leads in Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer (who do plenty of stunt work) . The show debuts later this week, and reviews are finally starting to roll in. Having seen the show in its entirety for myself, I figured there would be high praise for the visuals, but I am surprised by one particular critique amongst critics.

2099 – which, of course, takes place 50 years after 2017’s Blade Runner 2049 – sees Replicants having become the ruling class, while humans are treated like vermin. At the center of the story is Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human trying to escape her circumstances by posing as a Replicant Blade Runner. In the process of doing that, she is partnered with Olwen (Yeoh), a dying Replicant Runner. The story does indeed get dark, but I didn’t have much of an issue with it. As for The Guardian’s Rhik Samadder, though, he says:

Samadder also notably calls the visuals both “impressive” and “oppressive” in a way. However, also mentioning that the series also “plunges us into a far darker world” than the Blade Runner movies ( which don’t directly tie into 2099 ). Likewise, Aaron Pruner of CNET isn’t really a fan of the overly dark setting and aesthetic. In his somewhat mixed review, Pruner praises the show’s execution while also posing this question regarding the bleak vibe:

The darkness doesn’t seem to be deterring everyone, though, as Alison Herman of Variety has glowing thoughts on the show. Aside from praising Hunter Schafer, Herman also admires series creator Silka Luisa’s adherence to this storied continuity birthed by Philip K. Dick:

That’s definitely a big compliment, considering how beloved Ridley Scott ’s original 1982 film is and how much critical praise Denis Villeneuve’s 2049 received . Still, not everyone is impressed. TVLine’s Dave Nemetz finds the sci-fi show to be overly bleak as well. Not only that, but he also isn’t too taken with the visuals like a number of others are:

Although I can’t say I saw these critiques about the show’s vibe coming, I can’t blame others for not caring for its dark nature. To me, this kind of style is just baked into the DNA of the franchise, though I can admit that Blade Runner 2099 does delve into murkier territory at times. I’m curious as to how fans will feel when all eight episodes of the show become available for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25.
